stem: PLACEHOLDER SAMPLE. A possessor has openly farmed a parcel for 12 years in a jurisdiction with a 20-year statutory period. The prior possessor, who farmed it for 10 years, sold his interest to the current possessor by deed. Which element is most directly satisfied by adding the two periods together?
explanation: Tacking lets successive possessors in privity combine their periods of possession to meet the continuity requirement for the statutory period.

stem: PLACEHOLDER SAMPLE. Two squatters occupied the same cabin, one after the other, with no transfer between them. The second squatter claims adverse possession by tacking. What is the best response?
choices: Tacking is allowed because the possession was continuous in fact
Tacking is not allowed because there was no privity between the possessors
Tacking is allowed only if the first squatter consents in writing
Tacking is not allowed because squatters can never adversely possess
Tacking is allowed because both possessors were hostile
explanation: Tacking requires privity, meaning a voluntary transfer of the possessory interest between successive possessors. Sequential unrelated squatters lack privity.

stem: PLACEHOLDER SAMPLE. Under the Wisconsin statute, what is the general period of adverse possession when the claimant has no color of title and pays no taxes?
explanation: Wis. Stat. § 893.25 sets a 20-year period for adverse possession not founded on a written instrument. (Placeholder: verify against the current statute.)

stem: PLACEHOLDER SAMPLE. A claimant admits in a court filing that the record owner holds title to the disputed strip but asks to keep using it. This admission most directly undermines which element?
explanation: Acknowledging the true owner's superior title is inconsistent with possession under a claim of right, so the hostility element fails (as in Van Valkenburgh v. Lutz).

stem: PLACEHOLDER SAMPLE. Which of the following is generally NOT subject to adverse possession?
choices: Farmland owned by an absentee landlord
A strip of a neighbor's yard
explanation: Government-owned land is generally exempt from adverse possession claims.

factPattern:
PLACEHOLDER SAMPLE. In 2004 Dana began farming a strip of land along the edge of her neighbor Owen's parcel, believing it was hers. She fenced it, planted it every spring, and posted a sign reading "Dana's Field." In 2015 Dana sold her farm to Pat by warranty deed describing only Dana's own parcel; Pat kept farming the strip. In 2024 Owen returned from years abroad, discovered the fence, and sued Pat to quiet title. Pat counterclaims for title by adverse possession. Wisconsin law applies.

Discuss Pat's claim.

issues.name: Elements of adverse possession (actual, open and notorious, exclusive, hostile, continuous)
issues.modelAnalysis: Placeholder. Fencing, planting, and the sign show actual, open, and exclusive possession. Dana's mistaken belief does not defeat hostility under the objective view. The question is whether the possession has been continuous for the statutory period.

issues.name: Tacking between Dana and Pat
issues.modelAnalysis: Placeholder. Dana's deed did not describe the strip, so Pat must argue that privity exists through the voluntary transfer of possession of the strip along with the farm. If tacking is allowed, 2004 to 2024 satisfies a 20-year period; if not, Pat has only 9 years.

issues.name: Wisconsin statutory period
issues.modelAnalysis: Placeholder. Without color of title the period is 20 years under Wis. Stat. § 893.25. Dana's possession began in 2004, so the period ran in 2024 only if tacking succeeds. Verify against the current statute.

factPattern:
PLACEHOLDER SAMPLE. The State of Wisconsin owns a wooded lot next to Lee's cabin. For 25 years Lee has parked a camper on the lot each summer, cleared a fire pit, and told visitors the lot was "part of the place." Lee now claims title by adverse possession.

Identify the problems with Lee's claim.

issues.name: Government land exception
issues.modelAnalysis: Placeholder. Land owned by the state is generally not subject to adverse possession, which ends the claim regardless of the other elements.

issues.name: Continuity of seasonal use
issues.modelAnalysis: Placeholder. Even setting the exception aside, summer-only use can satisfy continuity only if it matches how an owner would use a wooded lot; a camper and fire pit may be enough for recreational land, but exclusivity is doubtful.
